You own ALL Entire work for the Suture neatHack entry, in C:\Users\DELL\suture (repo github.com/Sireadell/suture, public; keys are in the gitignored .env, never print or commit them). STANDING RULE from the founder: use Entire at every level, never add an outside tool for a job Entire can do, never ask permission to use a sponsor tool, if Entire falls short say exactly how. Do these in order, saving results under evidence/entire/ (small dated commits made DURING your session so each becomes a checkpoint; plain messages that say what changed, no AI or process wording, no Co-Authored-By, explicit file paths in git add, git pull --rebase before push; never touch suture/loop.py, README.md, hackathon.md or files other sessions own):
1. VERIFY THE PUBLIC LINK. Find out exactly how to get an accessible checkpoint link and ID for submission: link format https://entire.io/gh/Sireadell/suture/commit/<FULL_SHA>; confirm the repo is imported at entire.io, checkpoints are synced (entire status), the page is reachable logged out (public repo), and record the exact ID plus link in evidence/entire/CHECKPOINTS.md. Warn the founder if an org admin step or an hour of sync is still pending.
2. USE THE COMMANDS. Run and record real output (trim secrets, none expected) of: entire checkpoint list, entire checkpoint explain <id or HEAD>, entire search, entire recap, entire dispatch, entire activity, entire session list. Note any that fail or give nothing.
3. TRAILS, GRAPH, BRAIN. Read how Trails, Graph and Brain work and enable whatever fits this repo. Entire's own idea #1 for this hackathon is a debugger that traces a bug back to the checkpoint where the wrong assumption entered; the side prize is 'most creative use of Checkpoints, Graph or Brain'. Build a small, honest 'where the bug came from' view for Clerk: for the Clerk bugs (unknown order id falling back to order A1001, malformed requests answered 200), use Entire to name the session and checkpoint where the code was written (the Clerk file was written in a session recorded earlier; if no checkpoint exists for it, say so plainly, do not invent). Record in evidence/entire/WHERE_THE_BUG_CAME_FROM.md and say how it can be one column in a repair scoreboard.
4. GAPS. Keep evidence/entire/ENTIRE_NOTES.md: every Entire gap or bug with exact reproduction (e.g. link prompt blocks agent commits until commit_linking is set; OpenCode export gaps seen from another entrant in Discord are not ours). Include anything unclear in the docs.
5. Make sure your own commits create checkpoints and report the new count and IDs.
Report back concisely: what you did, results with IDs and links, and anything blocked. Do not run entire session attach.

332	# Capture Sessions and Their Checkpoints
333	
334	> Learn how Entire captures agent sessions and turns them into committed checkpoints.
335	
336	Entire captures session context while you work, then creates a committed checkpoint when that context is linked to a Git commit.
337	
338	## How Capture Works
339	
340	Checkpoint capture has two parts:
341	
342	1. [Agent hooks](/agents/overview) collect session context, including prompts, transcript, tool activity, changed files, and token usage when available.
343	2. Git hooks link that captured context to a commit by adding an [`Entire-Checkpoint` trailer](/glossary#entire-checkpoint).
344	
345	After the commit, Entire stores checkpoint metadata in your repository, in [its own Git ref or on the checkpoints branch](/security#where-your-data-lives) depending on the [storage backend](/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage). Your working branch stays clean.
346	
347	## Set Up Capture for an Agent
348	
349	For a new repository, enable Entire with the agent you use:
350	
351	```bash theme={null}
352	entire enable --agent AGENT
353	```
354	
355	For a repository where Entire is already enabled, add another agent:
356	
357	```bash theme={null}
358	entire agent add AGENT
359	```
360	
361	You can see the supported built-in agents in [Agents](/agents/overview), or run:
362	
363	```bash theme={null}
364	entire agent list
365	```
366	
367	## Commit After Agent Work
368	
369	To capture agent-assisted work in a checkpoint:
370	
371	1. Start your agent from an Entire-enabled repository.
372	2. Ask the agent to make a change.
373	3. Stage and commit the change with Git.
374	
375	```bash theme={null}
376	git add .
377	git commit -m "Describe the change"
378	```
379	
380	If Entire detects recent agent work, it may ask whether to link the commit to the session context. Choose `yes` to create the checkpoint. Choose `always` if you want Entire to remember that preference for future matching commits.
381	
382	```text theme={null}
383	Entire: Active Codex session detected
384	  Last prompt: Add a user settings page...
385	
386	Link this commit to session context?
387	  [Y]es / [n]o / [a]lways (remember my choice):
388	```
389	
390	## Link Future Commits Automatically
391	
392	When the "Link this commit to session context?" prompt appears during `git commit`, choosing `yes` or `no` only applies to that one commit.
393	
394	To link future matching commits in this repository without being prompted during `git commit`, set `commit_linking` to `always`.
395	
396	Set `commit_linking` in one of these files:
397	
398	* `.entire/settings.local.json` if this preference should only apply to you
399	* `.entire/settings.json` if this should be the team setting for the repository
400	
401	```json theme={null}
402	{
403	  "commit_linking": "always"
404	}
405	```
406	
407	## Let the Agent Commit
408	
409	Your agent can also create commits for you. For example, you might ask it to make a focused change and commit when it is done.
410	
411	Entire still uses the Git hooks to link the commit to the captured session context. If the agent makes several commits in one session, each commit gets its own checkpoint.
412	
413	## Capture Multiple Commits from One Session
414	
415	A single agent session can produce multiple checkpoints. This happens when a long session creates several commits, or when you split the agent's work into smaller commits yourself.
416	
417	Each commit gets its own checkpoint ID. The checkpoints can share the same session context so you can still inspect the prompts, transcript, and work that led to each commit.
418	
419	## Capture One Checkpoint from Multiple Sessions
420	
421	One checkpoint can also include more than one session. This happens when several agent sessions contribute to the work before you make a single commit.
422	
423	In entire.io, those sessions appear together inside the checkpoint's Sessions tab. The checkpoint diff shows the combined change, while [session details](/guides/sessions/sessions-in-entire-io) show the context behind each contribution.
424	
425	## What Does Not Create a Checkpoint
426	
427	Entire needs captured session context and a Git commit to create a normal committed checkpoint.
428	
429	A checkpoint may not appear when:
430	
431	* Entire has not been enabled in the repository
432	* agent hooks were not installed for the agent you used
433	* the agent did not change files in the repository
434	* no commit was created
435	* a GUI Git client could not find the `entire` command from its Git hooks
436	
437	If a checkpoint is missing or did not link where you expected, see [Troubleshooting](/guides/sessions/troubleshooting).

799	# Session Storage
800	
801	> Where Entire stores your session and the checkpoints that are linked with your commits.
802	
803	Entire stores checkpoints inside your own Git repository, separate from your source branches. Your code stays on your source branches, while prompts, transcripts, session context, and checkpoint metadata live in checkpoint storage. Most of this happens behind the scenes, so your workflow stays the same: you create, search, explain, and resume checkpoints with the same Entire commands regardless of how they are stored.
804	
805	<Note>
806	  We verified this page against **Entire CLI 0.10.2**. Run `entire version` to check what you have installed.
807	</Note>
808	
809	## Store Checkpoints with Your Code
810	
811	This is the default and needs no configuration. Entire stores checkpoint data in the same Git repository as your code and pushes it when you push, which keeps the commit, the checkpoint, and the agent context together while leaving your normal Git history clean.
812	
813	In a repository with several remotes, Entire elects one checkpoint sync remote rather than copying checkpoints everywhere you push. `entire status` names the destination and counts checkpoints that have not reached it.
814	
815	This can be changed if you want your checkpoint and session storage history to reside elsewhere:
816	
817	* [**Push checkpoints to a separate repository**](/guides/checkpoints/store-checkpoints-in-another-repo)
818	* [**Keep checkpoints local on your machine**](/guides/checkpoints/keep-checkpoints-local)
819	
820	## The Two Storage Backends
821	
822	The backend controls how Git organizes checkpoint data. It is a separate question from which repository receives that data.
823	
824	### Ref-Based Storage
825	
826	Ref-based storage (`git-refs`) is the default. It gives each new checkpoint its own Git ref, a named pointer inside your repository that Entire creates and manages for you. Each ref lives at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, and Entire saves and retrieves each checkpoint independently.
827	
828	**The benefit:** With ref-based storage, pushes and reads stay fast even as your repository accumulates more agent history. Multiple agents can also save their work at the same time without competing to update a shared branch.
829	
830	Ref-based checkpoints use 26-character, time-sortable ULIDs, such as `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`.
831	
832	Ref-based storage first shipped as an opt-in option in Entire CLI 0.8.42 and became the default in 0.10.0, where `entire enable` writes it during a first-time setup and no longer asks you to choose.
833	
834	### Branch-Based Storage
835	
836	Branch-based storage (`git-branch`) keeps every checkpoint on a shared Git branch called [`entire/checkpoints/v1`](/glossary#checkpoints-branch). Each checkpoint sits at `<first two characters of the ID>/<rest of the ID>/` in the branch tree.
837	
838	**The benefit:** All checkpoint history lives on one branch you can check out, browse, or clone like any other branch.
839	
840	Branch-based checkpoints use 12-character hexadecimal IDs, such as `a3b2c4d5e6f7`.
841	
842	A repository you enabled before Entire CLI 0.10.0 uses branch-based storage and stays on it until you [switch backends](#switch-backends).
843	
844	<span id="configure-checkpoint-storage" />
845	
846	## Find Which Backend a Repository Uses
847	
848	The backend is named by `checkpoints.primary.type` in `.entire/settings.json`, or in `.entire/settings.local.json` when someone set it for their clone alone. An absent `checkpoints` block resolves to `git-branch`, which is why a pre-0.10.0 repository keeps branch storage without any setting naming it.
849	
850	Checkpoint storage is ordinary Git, so Git reads it without Entire installed. List the per-checkpoint refs:
851	
852	```bash theme={null}
853	git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/
854	```
855	
856	Each line names one checkpoint, where `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID and `<id>` is always the leaf. Check for branch-backed checkpoints too:
857	
858	```bash theme={null}
859	git show-ref entire/checkpoints/v1
860	```
861	
862	Output from both means the repository holds checkpoints in both formats, which is the expected state after a backend switch. To confirm what reached the remote, run `git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'`.
863	
864	## Both Backends Stay Readable
865	
866	Every reader routes by ID format, so one repository can hold both formats at once. This holds for the CLI, entire.io, and the Entire API.
867	
868	| Checkpoint ID | Where the read goes |
869	| - | - |
870	| ULID | Refs only. ULIDs are minted only under ref-based storage |
871	| Hex, branch-based backend | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch |
872	| Hex, ref-based backend | Refs first, then the branch, since a hex checkpoint may still sit on the pre-switch branch |
873	
874	`entire checkpoint list` merges both backends and de-duplicates by ID. A new checkpoint goes to the configured backend, while a backfill that adds a transcript, summary, or attribution to an existing checkpoint lands in whichever backend already holds it.
875	
876	## Switch Backends
877	
878	To enable ref-based storage in a new repository, run:
879	
880	```bash theme={null}
881	entire enable --checkpoint-backend refs
882	```
883	
884	To enable it in an existing Entire-enabled repository, run:
885	
886	```bash theme={null}
887	entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
888	```
889	
890	Both commands accept `refs` and `branch`, plus the canonical `git-refs` and `git-branch` that settings store. Add `--local` when the choice should apply only to your clone.
891	
892	A switch applies to new checkpoints. Checkpoints written before the switch stay exactly where they are and keep resolving through the routing above, so `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain`, attribution, and entire.io continue to serve them. Entire deletes nothing during a switch, and your commands and commit workflow do not change.
893	
894	Two things do change after a switch to ref-based storage. New checkpoint IDs become ULIDs instead of hex, and the pre-push hook starts pushing queued per-checkpoint refs instead of the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Leave that branch on the remote: it is where readers find every checkpoint captured before the switch.
895	
896	## Migrate Existing Checkpoints into Refs
897	
898	Migration is optional, since the routing above already resolves branch-backed checkpoints under a ref-based backend. Migrate when you want the whole history in one format, or when you want to stop carrying the v1 branch.
899	
900	<Warning>
901	  Run the migration **before** you switch the backend to refs. The command refuses to run once ref-based storage is primary, because the refs are authoritative at that point and re-importing branch snapshots could only move them backwards.
902	</Warning>
903	
904	```bash theme={null}
905	entire doctor migrate-checkpoints --dry-run
906	entire doctor migrate-checkpoints
907	```
908	
909	The command wraps each checkpoint's current tree in a fresh commit and points its ref at it, keeping the hex ID as the ref name. It does not rewrite the branch commits, and it does not delete the branch. It skips checkpoints it has already converted, so you can re-run it after more branch activity.
910	
911	| Flag | Description |
912	| - | - |
913	| `--dry-run` | Report what would be migrated without writing refs |
914	| `--remote NAME` | Push migrated refs to this remote instead of the checkpoint sync remote |
915	
916	Migrated refs are queued for push. Run interactively, the command asks whether to push them now. Run without a terminal, it leaves them queued, and they flush on the next `git push` once ref-based storage is primary. Then switch and push:
917	
918	```bash theme={null}
919	entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
920	git push
921	```
922

925	## Auto-Generate Checkpoint Summaries
926	
927	Checkpoint metadata can carry a summary generated at commit time. Enable it with `strategy_options.summarize.enabled`:
928	
929	```json .entire/settings.json theme={null}
930	{
931	  "strategy_options": {
932	    "summarize": {
933	      "enabled": true
934	    }
935	  }
936	}
937	```
938	
939	Then choose the provider and model:
940	
941	```bash theme={null}
942	entire configure --summarize-provider PROVIDER
943	entire configure --summarize-model MODEL
944	```

946	## Where Storage Settings Are Saved
947	
948	`entire configure` writes to `.entire/settings.json` by default, so the repository shares the setting. Add `--local` to write `.entire/settings.local.json` instead, which applies only to your clone and takes precedence over project settings.
949	
950	The `checkpoints` block is a selection, not a merged document: a `checkpoints` block in `.entire/settings.local.json` replaces the one in `.entire/settings.json` outright. The `strategy_options` keys merge by layer as usual. See [Local, Project, and Global Settings](/guides/configuration/settings-layers) for the full table.

Entire Brain is a memory layer for your Git repository. Brain is great for team collaboration and individual work when you are context switching across tasks and agents. It helps you spend less time explaining your project and repeating earlier research. A new agent session can start with the decisions, rules, and lessons that has already been recorded. For example, before changing how failed requests are retried, you can ask Brain for earlier decisions about retries. Your agent can use that context to understand the current approach before editing the code. ## What Can You Do with Brain? * Understand a project to get an overview of its structure and how it works. * Prepare for a task and find relevant decisions, code locations, and possible tests. * Find earlier work by searching through saved facts, history, and documentation. * Record a project rule or decision for future sessions. * Use memory to browse what Brain knows in a local UI. ## Before You Start Use a local Git repository with at least one commit. Fact extraction uses an available coding agent, can send session content to its model provider, and can incur token charges. The watcher can continue extracting facts over time.
